timeline.text: Alan Brooks presents with confusion and ataxia. The Chief Concern card lists confusion, ataxia, and abnormal eye movements.
The nurse notes nystagmus and chronic alcohol use with poor nutrition. Pain and SpO2 are documented in the vital signs card.
New results show magnesium is 1.4 mg/dl and glucose is 64 mg/dl. The findings support wernicke encephalopathy from thiamine deficiency.
Orders include administer thiamine before glucose-containing fluids if possible and assess airway and fall risk. The nurse avoids give glucose first without thiamine consideration when avoidable.
Initial treatment is underway and the client is reassessed. The priority response shows early clinical improvement.
Final evaluation shows improvement while unresolved risks remain. Ongoing follow-up is needed because in malnourished alcohol use, thiamine comes before glucose when possible.

timeline.text: Priya Shah presents with heavy lochia saturating pads and boggy uterus that firms then relaxes. The Chief Concern card lists heavy bleeding two hours after birth.
The nurse notes placenta had missing cotyledon and tachycardia and dizziness. Pain and SpO2 are documented in the vital signs card.
New results show hemoglobin drops from 11.4 to 8.9 g/dl and ultrasound shows echogenic retained tissue. The findings support postpartum hemorrhage likely related to retained products.
Orders include massage fundus and assess tone and notify provider and quantify blood loss. The nurse avoids leave client alone to rest.
Initial treatment is underway and the client is reassessed. The priority response shows early clinical improvement.
Final evaluation shows improvement while unresolved risks remain. Ongoing follow-up is needed because retained placental tissue can keep the uterus from staying contracted.

timeline.text: Victoria Hill presents with placenta previa with prior cesareans and prenatal imaging suspicious for accreta. The Chief Concern card lists planned cesarean with placenta previa and suspected accreta.
The nurse notes attempted placental separation causes heavy bleeding and uterus fails to separate placenta normally. Pain and SpO2 are documented in the vital signs card.
New results show estimated blood loss reaches 1800 ml and fibrinogen begins falling. The findings support placenta accreta spectrum with massive hemorrhage risk.
Orders include activate hemorrhage protocol and prepare blood products and large-bore access. The nurse avoids pull placenta forcefully to speed delivery.
Initial treatment is underway and the client is reassessed. The priority response shows early clinical improvement.

Final evaluation shows improvement while unresolved risks remain. Ongoing follow-up is needed because accreta hemorrhage is anticipated but still dangerous, and forceful placental removal can worsen bleeding.
